rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The destroyed towns are those of ʿĀd, Thamūd, Midian, Lot’s people, and their counterparts.
rows.anchor: الماضية من عاد وثمود ومدين وقوم لوط وأشكالهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He allows two readings of when they were destroyed: at the first wrongdoing, or after respite until their wrongdoing reached its limit.
rows.anchor: أهلكناهم بالفعل حين ظلمهم لكن لا في أوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their destruction had a fixed appointed time and place that God did not miss.
rows.anchor: وقتا نحله بهم فيه ومكانا لم نخلفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning also points to appointed worldly punishments for the present audience at Badr, the conquest, and Hunayn, and to the afterlife.
rows.anchor: في الدنيا بيوم بدر والفتح وحنين ونحو ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophet’s statement explicitly conveyed from God cannot fail, although God could choose otherwise; the certainty concerns what He has promised.
rows.anchor: كل أمر يقوله نبي من الأنبياء عنا لا يقع فيه خلف وإن كان يجوز لنا ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A prophet’s own statement not attributed to God can fail; he cites a forty-night delay or shorter caused by taking tomorrow literally.
rows.anchor: بخلاف ما يقوله من نفسه غير مسند إلينا فإنه يمكن وقوع الخلف فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After resurrection, creation, its signs, and divine forbearance, the narrative turns to Moses and Khidr: God appoints a sign and meeting while every event remains measured.
rows.anchor: فذكر قصة موسى مع الخضر عليهما السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fish’s extraordinary revival serves as evidence for resurrection and marks Moses’s appointed meeting with Khidr.
rows.anchor: مع ما فيها من الخارق الدال على البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story teaches that one should not challenge a person known for virtue and knowledge without confidence that one speaks from God, nor test him without warrant.
rows.anchor: على ثفة مما يقوله من ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative condemns disputation without knowledge and requires submission to truth once its proof becomes clear.
rows.anchor: الإرشاد إلى ذم الجدل بغير علم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses’s willingness to follow Khidr rebukes anyone who disdains sitting with poor believers to learn.
rows.anchor: ومن إرشاد من استنكف أن يجالس فقراء المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story answers Jews who told Quraysh that failure to answer their questions would prove Muhammad was no prophet: Moses himself lacked knowledge of Khidr’s acts.
rows.anchor: مع ما يعلمون من أن موسى عليه السلام خفي عليه جمع ما فعله الخضر عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses is identified as Moses son of ʿImrān, and his young companion is Joshua son of Nun.
rows.anchor: ابن عمران المرسل إلى بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses vows to keep traveling until he reaches the meeting of the two seas, the point he understood to be the starting place of his search for Khidr.
rows.anchor: لا أزال سائرا في طلب العبد الذي أعلمني ربي بفضله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If he does not find the appointed meeting there, Moses will continue for a long period.
rows.anchor: إن لم أظفر بمجمع البحرين الذي جعله ربي موعدا لي في لقائه

rows.speaker: القاموس
rows.claim: Al-Qāmūs defines ḥuqb as eighty years or more, a long age, a year, or years.
rows.anchor: قال في القاموس - ثمانون سنة أو أكثر والدهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meeting of the two waters alludes to a meeting of two seas of knowledge; the fish is linked to the letter nūn, the Pen, and the spring of life because knowledge revives hearts.
rows.anchor: وما أنسب التوقيت بمجمع بحري الماء بمجمع بحري العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two seas had become one body of water, so there was no intervening space between them at the meeting point.
rows.anchor: فلم يكن هناك بين أصلا لصيرورتهما شيئا واحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses failed to notice the fish’s state and forgot to ask about it; Joshua saw something of what happened but forgot to tell Moses.
rows.anchor: فنسي شيئا من حاله ونسي أن يسأل عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fish’s path through the sea was a miracle within a miracle; sarab means a broad, visible, unclosed opening, like a burrow or underground channel.
rows.anchor: أي خرقا في الماء غير ملتئم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report in the Ṣaḥīḥ says God revived the fish and held the water away from its track, leaving an arch that did not close.
rows.anchor: وقد ورد في حديثه في الصحيح أن الله تعالى أحياه وأمسك عن موضع جريه في الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meeting place may have stretched along the shore; Moses may have thought the goal lay farther ahead or that another confluence was intended.
rows.anchor: فظن موسى عليه السلام أن المطلوب أمامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses did not feel fatigue until after passing the appointed spot, which the author counts as another miracle; hunger then prompted his request for their breakfast.
rows.anchor: حتى جاوز المكان الذي أمربه معجزة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase this journey singles out that day’s travel, and the fish had been their provision but was now missing.
rows.anchor: أي الذي سافرناه في هذا اليوم خاصة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Joshua says he forgot to report the fish’s affair at the rock; the fish had revived and slipped from the basket into the sea.
rows.anchor: أي نسيت أن أذكر لك أمره الذي كان هناك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interruption and repetition in the wording heighten the wonder of the lapse.
rows.anchor: التعجيب من هذا النسيان بالاعتراض بين الإخبار به مجملا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan’s influence here did not make Joshua lose an obligation; the event instead elevated both travelers through fatigue at the destination and other signs.
rows.anchor: أن هذا الإنساء ليس مفوتا لطاعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reads 16:100 as limiting Satan’s authority to inducing sin, not causing this harmless lapse.
rows.anchor: مبين أن السلطان الحمل على المعاصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode includes the fish’s revival and the restoration of what had already been eaten from it.
rows.anchor: وقد كان في هذه القصة خوارق حياة الحوت وإيجاد ما كان أكل منه

rows.speaker: أسامة بن زيد
rows.claim: On the return from pilgrimage, the Prophet repeatedly asked a woman for a foreleg from her cooked sheep; when told there were only two, he said another could have been produced had she stayed silent.
rows.anchor: عن أسامة بن زيد رضي الله عنهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author compares the possible creation of another cooked foreleg with the fish’s revival as evidence that God’s word is true in both the unseen and witnessed realms.
rows.anchor: لو سكت أوجد الله لها ذراعا ثم ذراعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poisoned foreleg that informed the Prophet of its poison was a greater miracle than restoring life to the fish without speech.
rows.anchor: فهو أعظم من عود الحياة من غير نطق

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī argues that the Prophet’s moaning pulpit trunk was a greater sign than Jesus’s raising the dead.
rows.anchor: قال لي الشافعي : ما أعطى الله نبيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trunk’s moan, a stone’s greeting, pebbles’ glorification, and a door threshold and walls’ testimony exceed the fish’s return to life.
rows.anchor: حنين الجذع , وسلام الحجر , وتسبيح الحصا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He points to other revival signs for Abraham, the Prophet, and some members of the Prophet’s community, discussed earlier in Āl ʿImrān and al-Baqara.
rows.anchor: أشياء من إحياء الموتى له صلى الله عليه وعلى آله وسلم ولبعض أمته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The water sign is its refusal to close over the fish’s track; this is no less an instance of solidity than water resisting an opening in the first place.
rows.anchor: ولا فرق بين جموده بعدم الالتئام بعد الانخراق وبين جموده وصلابته بالامتناع من الانخراق

rows.speaker: أنس
rows.claim: A disconnected report says a deceased migrant woman’s son revived after her prayer and lived until the Prophet’s death; the author calls it a sign and notes the chain is interrupted.
rows.anchor: بسند منقطع عن أنس رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: During ʿUmar’s campaign, al-ʿAlāʾ prayed for rain and led the army across a sea channel with water reaching only their mounts’ hooves.
rows.anchor: واستعمل عليه العلاء بن الحضرمي

rows.speaker: بعض أصحاب الأعمش
rows.claim: A report describes Muslim horsemen crossing the flooded Tigris on horseback, frightening the Persians into flight; they lost only a cup attached to a saddle.
rows.anchor: عن الأعمش عن بعض أصحابه , قال :

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم الخولاني
rows.claim: Abū Muslim al-Khawlānī walks on the Tigris and asks whether any baggage is missing so they can pray.
rows.anchor: أبا مسلم الخولاني جاء إلى الدجلة وهي ترمي بالخشب من مده

rows.speaker: البيهقي
rows.claim: Al-Bayhaqī explicitly grades the report of Abū Muslim walking on the Tigris as sound.
rows.anchor: قال البيهقي : هذا إسناد صحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fish’s disappearance was the hidden sign they sought: it marked the appointed meeting with Khidr.
rows.anchor: الأمر العظيم من فقد الحوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Following their tracks suggests sandy terrain without footprints; he tentatively locates the meeting near the Nile’s outlet and the sea at Damietta or Rashid.
rows.anchor: أن الأرض كانت رملان لا علم فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author supports a Rashid location by the hadith’s bird dipping into the sea, since birds do not drink salt water, and by local lore about a half-sided fish; he remains uncertain.
rows.anchor: ويؤيده نقر العصفور في البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The servant is Khidr, named as belonging to God’s exalted presence; the majority hold that he was a prophet.
rows.anchor: وكونه نبيا قول الجمهور

rows.speaker: الحرالي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥarālī distinguishes ʿinda for what is manifest from ladun for what is hidden; here mercy is outward signs and knowledge is a hidden gift specific to God’s presence.
rows.anchor: وقال الأستاذ أبو الحسن الحرالي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sufis call knowledge received through unveiling ladunnī knowledge and describe spiritual discipline as preparing the soul for divine illumination without deliberation.
rows.anchor: فأهل التصوف سموا العلم بطريق المكاشفة العلم اللدني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses asks permission with courtesy and tact, offering to accompany Khidr wherever he goes.
rows.anchor: طالبا منه على سبيل التأدب والتلطف بإظهار ذلك في قالب الاستئذان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By asking to learn some of what Khidr was taught, Moses requests key principles that can guide him to the rest rather than all of Khidr’s knowledge.
rows.anchor: لا يطلب جميع ما عنده ليطول عليه الزمان بل جوامع منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passive in what you were taught leaves God as the understood teacher and signals that everything is easy for Him.
rows.anchor: بأن الفاعل هو الله سبحانه وتعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses seeks knowledge that guides him to right judgment; a prophet’s learning from another prophet is no deficiency, and the author affirms this is Moses son of ʿImrān based on the Ṣaḥīḥ.
rows.anchor: ولا نقص في تعلم نبي من نبي حتى يدعى أن موسى هذا ليس موسى بن عمران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr warns that Moses will not sustain the required full patience because the outward law will press him to object to acts whose inner grounds he cannot see.
rows.anchor: هو من العظمة على ما أريد لما يحثك على عدم الصبر من ظاهر الشرع الذي أمرت به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A teacher should warn a student firmly when useful, since silence could foster pride and obstruct learning.
rows.anchor: يوقع المتعلم في الغرور والنخوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr intensifies his warning by asking how Moses could be patient at all, rather than merely denying a particular kind of patience; the author excuses both men by the difference between outward and inward grounds.
rows.anchor: على وجه أبلغ من نفي الأخص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Not encompassing an event’s full meaning leaves open that Khidr is right inwardly, but does not remove Moses’s outward duty; alternatively, this explains why he cannot bear what looks wrong.
rows.anchor: فأشار بالإحاطة إلى أنه كان يجوز أن يكون على صواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses answers with humility, offering an example of how to seek knowledge and hoping God will make learning beneficial and easy.
rows.anchor: آتيا بنهاية التواضع لمن هو أعلم منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The future marker strengthens Moses’s promise, and adding God willing invokes the divine condition taught elsewhere in the surah and models the prophets’ way.
rows.anchor: قوى تأكيده بالتبرك بذكر الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses promises patience only where patience is lawful and says he will not disobey an instruction that does not conflict with God’s manifest command.
rows.anchor: على ما يجوز الصبر عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conjunction in Moses’s vow emphasizes his settled commitment both to patience and to avoiding disobedience.
rows.anchor: لبيان التمكن في كل من الوصفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr asks Moses not to question anything he says or does until Khidr himself explains its sound, permissible basis.
rows.anchor: فإني لا أقدم على شيء إلا هو صواب جائز في نفس الأمر وإن كان ظاهره غير ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After agreeing, Moses and Khidr travel along the shore looking for a boat to board.
rows.anchor: يطلبان سفينة يركبان فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses objects because the hole appears to destroy property and risk the greater harm of drowning the passengers; forbidding an apparent wrong is an immediate duty.
rows.anchor: لما في ظاهره من الفساد بإتلاف المال المفضي إلى فساد أكبر منه بإهلاك النفوس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He forgets their agreement under the urgency of his duty to condemn what looks wrong; the author says he would have objected even without forgetting because such an objection was excluded by the agreement’s terms.
rows.anchor: كما فعل عند قتل الغلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase that Khidr came with an imr describes an enormous, grave, astonishing wrong as it appeared to Moses.
rows.anchor: أي عظيما منكرا عجيبا شديدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr repeats his earlier warning after Moses’s first objection.
rows.anchor: فذكره بما قال له عند الشرط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses asks Khidr not to punish the lapse or make their journey intolerably difficult by ending the companionship prematurely.
rows.anchor: بالمؤاخذة على النسيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both are truthful according to their own knowledge: Moses never meant to agree to suppress what he sees as wrong, while Khidr’s promise concerns the act’s true nature and he never commits a wrong.
rows.anchor: فكل منهما صادق فيما قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses showed some patience by stopping after the reminder, but not the full silence Khidr expected at the first and final events.
rows.anchor: لأنه لما ذكره كف عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb for boring the boat is not prefixed by fa because the damage was neither caused by boarding nor done immediately upon boarding.
rows.anchor: بالفاء لأنه لم يكن مسببا عن الركوب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boy had not reached puberty and was exceptionally strong; the fa in the narrative indicates Khidr killed him as soon as he met him.
rows.anchor: لم يبلغ الحلم وهو في غاية القوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses calls the boy pure because he was still on original nature and had committed no sin deserving death, and stresses he had not killed another person in retaliation.
rows.anchor: بكونها على الفطرة الأولى من غير أن تدنس بخطيئة توجب القتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author infers from the retaliation wording that the boy may have been legally adult, unless their law allowed retaliation without puberty.
rows.anchor: أمكن أمكن قتله به إلا أن يكون شرعهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses marks this second objection more strongly: killing is direct, while boring the boat only indirectly risked drowning.
rows.anchor: وصرح بالإنكار في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr makes explicit that this is the second time and adds for you to his warning; Moses’s response is marked by embarrassment and regret.
rows.anchor: وزاد قوله : { لك إنك } يا موسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses says that another question will end their companionship, acknowledging his two breaches and Khidr’s forbearance; God had informed him of Khidr’s excellent state.
rows.anchor: وأعلم بشدة ندمه على الإنكار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the settlement a qarya rather than a madina suits the rebuke because the root evokes gathering and withholding, suggesting stinginess.
rows.anchor: عبر عنها هنا بالقرية دون المدينة لأنه أدل على الذم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit repetition of its people signals that those asked for food were some of those they had encountered, or a different subset; the author regards this as the customary reading.
rows.anchor: أوكل من الإتيان والاستطعام لبعض ولكنه غير متحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author applies al-Ḥarālī’s account of explicit nouns and pronouns to the verse: the wording distinguishes the people asked from those first approached.
rows.anchor: ومن نحوه { أتيا أهل قرية استطعما أهلها }

rows.speaker: السبكي
rows.claim: Al-Subkī says they visited some residents but asked all the residents for food, which he views as harsher blame and stronger evidence of bad character.
rows.anchor: وجعل السبكي الإتيان للبعض , والاستطعام للكل

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī treats the verse as a general wording narrowed by specification: Moses and Khidr did not ask every resident.
rows.anchor: قول الشافعي في كتاب الرسالة في باب ما نزل من الكتاب عاما يراد به العام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author supports the view that they asked only some residents: repeating an explicit noun instead of a pronoun distinguishes the people asked from those they visited.
rows.anchor: فلما عدل عنه - مع أنه أخصر -

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The residents refused to host the two travelers; describing the wall as being in the town rather than among the people further characterizes the settlement’s bad nature.
rows.anchor: أي فتسبب عن استطهامهما أن أبى المستطعمون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wall was about to fall quickly; Khidr set it upright by passing his hand over it.
rows.anchor: أي يسقط سريعا فمسحه الخضر بيده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses does not reproach Khidr this time; he offers that they could have taken payment for repairing the wall since the residents gave them nothing.
rows.anchor: فلم يعترض عليه في هذه المرة لعدم ما ينكر فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr calls the moment or the question their separation, making the cause or occasion stand for the separation itself.
rows.anchor: سبب الفراق أو محله , سماه به مبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase firaq bayni wa-baynika refers to the end of their companionship or to the parting of their exchange; the author also explains it through ellipsis as separation in both directions.
rows.anchor: وفراق بينك من بيني كما شرطت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author rejects interpreting firaq as connection: connection and separation cannot have one meaning, and bayn denotes the intervening space divided between the two parties.
rows.anchor: زوال الفصل ووجود الوصل , كذبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr’s three acts recall Moses’s analogous experiences: the damaged boat and the basket sent into the Nile both appeared fatal but brought safety from an oppressor.
rows.anchor: بخرق السفينة الذي ظاهره هلك وباطنه نجاة من يد الغاصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boy’s killing recalls Moses killing the Egyptian, even though Moses then did not know the divine command or full context.
rows.anchor: وبقتل الغلام على أنه كان معصوم الحركة في نفس الأمر في قتله القبطي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repairing the wall without pay recalls Moses watering Shuʿayb’s daughters without payment despite his need.
rows.anchor: وبإقامة الجدار من غير أجر على سقيه لبنات شعيب عليهم السلام من غير أجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taʾwīl means returning an event to its underlying wisdom; apparent and hidden harms conflict, and the lesser may be incurred to prevent the greater once that judgment is certain.
rows.anchor: لمخالفته عندك الحكمة إلى الحكمة وهو أن عند تعارض الضررين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The owners are miskīn poor people who work at sea; their ownership of a boat supports al-Shāfiʿī’s view that faqīr is poorer than miskīn.
rows.anchor: وهو دليل للشافعي على أن الفقير أسوأ حالا من المسكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr attributes the boat’s defect to himself as a mark of proper courtesy toward God.
rows.anchor: أسنده إليه خاصة , تأدبا مع الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A temporary loss of use and repair work is a lesser harm than losing the entire vessel to royal seizure; Khidr did not intend to drown its passengers.
rows.anchor: فإن تفويت منفعتها بذلك ساعة من نهار وتكليف أهلها لوحا يسدونها به أخف ضررا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Warāʾah means ahead in their direction here, and can suggest the king’s reach in every direction; al-Ḥarālī also uses it for what is beyond sense or knowledge, even when spatially ahead.
rows.anchor: وفسره الحرالي في سورة البقرة بأنه وراءهم في غيبته عن علمهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The king confiscated every sound vessel at that time, and the owners did not know of the danger.
rows.anchor: من أصحابها ولم يكن عند أصحابها علم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author foregrounds the boat owners’ poverty because compassion for them is the stronger of the two motives for damaging the vessel.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى أن أقوى السببين الحاملين على فعله الرأفة بالمساكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khidr says the boy’s parents were believers and that the boy himself was innately disposed to unbelief, as the hadith from Ubayy will explain.
rows.anchor: على الكفر - كما يأتي في حديث أبي رضي الله عنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the boy grew up, his attachment or harsh boldness might overwhelm his parents with tyranny and disbelief, damaging their worldly life or religious faith.
rows.anchor: إن كبر بمحبتهما له أو بجراءته وقساوته

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report from Ibn ʿAbbās through Ubayy says the boy Khidr killed was created a disbeliever and would have driven his parents into tyranny and disbelief if he lived.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس عن أبي بن كعب رضي الله عنه أن النبي صلى الله عليه وعلى آله وسلم قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reads the report about what they would have done as indicating that hypothetical punishment applies to innate disposition, not a merely contingent condition.
rows.anchor: إنما يكون على ما كان جبلة وطبعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural we refers to Khidr’s action under God’s command; God alone replaces the boy, as the shift to your Lord indicates.
rows.anchor: التعويض عن هذا الولد لله وحده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zakāh means greater purity and blessing: the boy seemed pure at that moment but would have become corrupt in the future.
rows.anchor: من جهة كونه كان ظاهر الزكاء في الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The replacement might mean patience or another child; the transmitted account says the parents received a daughter.
rows.anchor: يمكن أن يكون الصبر , ويمكن أن يكون ولدا آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aqraba raḥman means more dutiful, affectionate, and merciful toward the parents; their grief was less harmful than the boy’s future damage to their faith or life.
rows.anchor: برا بهما وعطفا عليهما ورحمة لهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the boys orphans shows they were still below adulthood.
rows.anchor: على كونهما دون البلوغ بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qarya and madīna are compatible: qarya suits the criticism of hoarding, while madīna evokes inhabitants who could witness the wall fall and take the treasure.
rows.anchor: وكانت المدينة بمعنى الإقامة , فكان التعبير بها أليق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wall was repaired without payment so the buried wealth would not be lost when the wall collapsed; the treasure was stored money belonging to the orphans.
rows.anchor: لو وقع لكان أقرب إلى ضياعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The father’s righteousness merited care for his descendants; righteous parents’ conduct can preserve their children’s interests.
rows.anchor: ينبغي مراعاته وخلفه في ذريته بخير

rows.speaker: الحسن بن علي
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī told a Kharijite that God protected the boys’ treasure because of their father’s righteousness; when the man praised his own forebears, al-Ḥasan answered that God called them contentious.
rows.anchor: روي عن الحسن بن علي رضي الله عهنما أنه قال لبعض الخوارج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God alone is credited with bringing the boys to maturity and enabling them to recover the treasure; Moses’s Lord had similarly cared for him while orphaned.
rows.anchor: ولما كان الإبلاغ إلى حد البلوغ والاستخراج فعل الله وحده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The free wall repair was a mercy to the orphans, since the cost of the repair was less harmful than losing the treasure.
rows.anchor: فكان التعب في إقامة الجدار مجانا أدنى من الضرر اللازم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion states that Khidr acted only by God’s order, not on his own initiative.
rows.anchor: بل عن أمر من له الأمر , وهو الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The shortened form tasṭiʿ omits a tāʾ because after the veil is lifted the matter is bearable; if Moses had known it from the outset, he could not have objected in the same way.
rows.anchor: منكره غير صابر أصلا لو كان عنده مكشوفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reconciles Solomon’s failed plan for a hundred warrior sons with Moses’s conduct: the sacrifice was an explicit divine command, whereas Moses objected to acts whose divine basis was hidden from him.
rows.anchor: فإن الذبيح صبر على ما هو قاطع بأنه بعينه أمر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses obeyed the outward law he knew, and once reminded that God approved Khidr’s actions, he stopped objecting; this preserved his status among the great messengers.
rows.anchor: أنه وفي بمقام الشرع الذي أقامه الله فيه

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet’s wish that Moses had waited meant he wished Moses had delayed agreeing to Khidr’s request to part, not that Moses should have ignored his duty to object.
rows.anchor: صبر عن الإذن للخضر عليه السلام في مفارقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Muslim narration says that had Moses not hurried, he would have seen more wonders, but shame toward his companion overcame him.
rows.anchor: لولا أنه عجل لرأى العجب

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A Bukhārī report through Ibn ʿAbbās and Ubayy recounts Moses asking whether anyone was more learned, God’s correction, the fish sign, Khidr’s identity question, the boat, and the bird’s comparison of their knowledge with God’s.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وعلى آله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bird’s tiny sip from the sea illustrates how little Moses’s and Khidr’s knowledge removes from God’s knowledge.
rows.anchor: ما نقص علمي وعلمك من علم الله إلا كما نقص هذا البحر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hadith distinguishes knowledge that Moses could not properly act upon from the inward knowledge Khidr followed; each had knowledge the other should not use.
rows.anchor: أي لا ينبغي لك أن تعمل بالباطن ولا ينبغي لي أنا أن أقف مع الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The story urges prompt public command of right and endurance in it, without deferring for rank or age when one trusts the outward evidence of revelation and religious authorities.
rows.anchor: بالمبادرة بالأمر بالمعروف والنهي عن المنكرو المصابرة عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Neither a prophet nor a saint with ladunnī knowledge knows everything; the report even has Khidr ask Moses who he is.
rows.anchor: لأن الخضر سأل موسى عليهما السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Dhul Qarnayn story follows Moses and Khidr as a journey across the earth for jihad after a journey for knowledge, giving precedence to knowledge as the basis of success and affairs.
rows.anchor: وقدم الأولى إشارة إلى علو درجة العلم لأنه أساس كل سعادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhul Qarnayn is called a righteous warrior; proposed explanations of his name include courage, reaching the western and eastern horizons, two generations dying in his era, braids, or a two-horned crown.
rows.anchor: سمي لشجاعته أو لبلوغه

rows.speaker: ابن كثير
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr transmits from al-Azraqī that Alexander the First lived in Abraham’s time and circumambulated the Kaʿba with him.
rows.anchor: نقل ابن كثير عن الأزرقي أنه كان على زمن الخليل عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two stories have a formal parallel: each presents three episodes, ending in construction of an unsheltered wall to protect something valuable from corruption.
rows.anchor: ومن المناسبات الصورية أن في قصة كل منهما ثلاثة أشياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beginning with the question rebukes the Jews for not asking about the preceding story if they sought truth; if they did not, their conduct deserves still greater reproach.
rows.anchor: تبكيتا لليهود في إغفال الأمر بالسؤال عنها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, this question may connect back to their first question about the Spirit, with the separated questions linked like pearls on a string.
rows.anchor: أو تكون معطوفة على مسألتهم الأولى وهي الروح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad is told to promise a connected account in the future only if God informs him, following the earlier instruction to say God willing.
rows.anchor: أي أقص قصا متتابعا في مستقبل الزمان إن أعلمني الله به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account gives the audience enough to know Dhul Qarnayn and the essential points of his story, which demonstrate God’s greatness.
rows.anchor: في تعرف أمره , جامعا لمجامع ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say God established Dhul Qarnayn through kingship alone; others say with prophethood as well. The author favors reading the divine favor at its fullest, especially with the majestic wording.
rows.anchor: قيل : بالملك وحده , وقيل مع النبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God enabled him to travel through the earth and prevail over its kings, and supplied the means needed for his aims.
rows.anchor: يصل بها إلى جميع مسلوكها

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says sabab originally meant rope and broadened to mean whatever one uses to reach an aim.
rows.anchor: قال أبو حيان : وأصل السبب الحبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, and Abū ʿAmr read atbaʿa with shadda, meaning he pursued; the other readers read it with a hamza and silent tāʾ, meaning he joined means together, which the author treats as an explanation of the first reading.
rows.anchor: على قراءة ابن كثير ونافع وأبي عمرو بالتشديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The western destination is the furthest limit humans can reach westward, not a claim that the sun literally enters a spring; from the shore, sight and touch make it appear to set there as it appears to set into the sea.
rows.anchor: الحد الذي لا يتجاوزه آدمي في جهة الغرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spring is muddy and hot, and the people beside it are powerful unbelievers.
rows.anchor: أي ذات حمأة أي طين أسود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The divine address to Dhul Qarnayn may come through an angel if he was a prophet, through a prophet of his era, or through sound judgment in his religious law; the first is most apparent.
rows.anchor: إما بواسطة الملك إن كان نبيا وهو أظهر الاحتمالات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although killing is permitted, the better course is to begin by calling the people to faith and use force only after hope of their return is gone.
rows.anchor: إشارة إلى أن القتل وإن كان جائزا فالأولى أن لا يفعل إلا بعد اليأس من الرجوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhul Qarnayn says he will first deal gently with persistent wrongdoers, then kill them once they are beyond hope; their punishment is severe for ingratitude and worshipping another instead of their benefactor.
rows.anchor: فإنا نرفق به حتى نيأس منه ثم نقتله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The threat rebukes Jews who misled Quraysh and directs Quraysh to ask about resurrection.
rows.anchor: وفي ذلك إشارة بالتهديد الشديد لليهود الغارين لقريش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers who act rightly receive the best reward in both worlds, and after examining their deeds Dhul Qarnayn will give them manageable orders such as prayer, alms, tax, and jihad.
rows.anchor: أي قولا غير شاق من الصلاة والزكاة والخراج والجهاد وغيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He next follows a route from the south toward the east and presses onward to the first inhabited land reached by sunrise.
rows.anchor: من جهة الجنوب يوصله إلى المشرق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The eastern people live exposed by the sea; no mountain, buildings, trees, or other barrier shelters them from the sun’s first rising.
rows.anchor: من جبل ولا أبنية ولا شجر ولا غيرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God has complete knowledge of every hidden and visible detail of Dhul Qarnayn’s affairs, so neither this account nor the cave story or Spirit should seem surprising; He relates only what wisdom calls for.
rows.anchor: فلا تستغرب إخبارنا عن ذلك ولا عن أمر أصحاب الكهف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhul Qarnayn next takes a northern route toward the barrier and the outlet of Gog and Magog.
rows.anchor: في إرادته ناحية السد مخرج يأجوج ومأجوج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two barriers are mountain ranges blocking passage in both directions, near the edge of Turkic lands by Armenia and Azerbaijan; their surfaces are smooth and slippery.
rows.anchor: وهما بمنقطع أرض الترك مما يلي بلاد أرمينية وآذربيجان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, and Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim read al-saddayn with fatḥa on the sīn; the remaining readers use ḍamma.
rows.anchor: قرأ ابن كثير وأبو عمرو وحفص
